newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBA alleviates Australian bond supply squeeze.
newsitem.headline: RBA alleviates Australian bond supply squeeze.

text.p: *The RBA's announcement that it was cutting commercial bank's prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements was seen alleviating a potential supply squeeze in the government bond market.
*Large rise expected in April housing finance due Wednesday.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's announcement that it was cutting commercial bank's prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements to 3.0 percent was seen alleviating a potential supply squeeze in the government bond market.

Under the old PAR requirements banks were required to hold an amount equal to six percent of their liabilities in high quality, readily cashable assets, including notes and coins, and Federal government securities.
"It's reflecting likely rundown in new supply from the Federal government, and helps to alleivate that squeeze," said David Bassanese, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.

The RBA also said that state government bonds, or semis, could also be included in PAR, a move that had been rumoured in the semis market since the government projected a further easing off in supply in last month's budget.
Semis spreads to government bond narrowed slightly on the announcement, although it had already been largely priced in.

Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia, said that at a rough estimate there was some A$23 billion of federal stock held under the old PAR arrangement, so conceivably this could come back to A$12 billion.
However, Roberts pointed out that the RBA said it would be holding discussions with each bank to agree a liquidity management approach over the coming months.
"It's not all going to happen on June 23, so the impact should be muted," he added.
The RBA also said that the PAR changes would not have any impact on monetary policy.
Meanwhile, the bond market closed firm, largely holding gains made in after hours trading late on Friday on the tail of a rally in U.S. Treasuries and in front of yesterday's local holiday.
The focus now centres on this week's key data for housing finance on Wednesday and the labour force report on Thursday.
A large jump is expected in April housing finance, and a key issue will be how much of 12 percent rise economists are expecting is fresh mortgages as opposed to refinancings.
Today's release of the ANZ May job advertisements provided a prelude to Thursday's data, although the 7.3 percent fall was largely seen as a correction to the 16.7 percent rise in April.
However, a weak outcome to the official data on Thursday is likely to stoke up thoughts of a further easing in monetary policy, analysts added.

The local market showed a narrowing bias to the dollar bloc, particularly against New Zealand which camne under pressure in the face of a weak N.Z. TWI. The yield curve flattened slightly as the long-end benefitted more from the net advance in U.S. Treasuries either side of the weekend.
